newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - FINANCIAL TIMES - JUNE 19.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - FINANCIAL TIMES - JUNE 19.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. -- GAS CHARGES TO BE CUT AS MMC BACKS WATCHDOG

The Monopolies and Mergers Commission has backed the demand made by UK gas regulators for BG's Transco subsidiary to cut charges for its pipeline transmission. Clare Spottiswoode of Ofgas announced the 19 million domestic gas customers are set to receive an initial one-off cut of 29 sterling from an average bill of 325 sterling that will be followed by additional cuts leading to reductions of 54 stg per year by the end of the pricing formula period.
-- BAE and LOCKHEED IN $100 BILLION FIGHTER PROJECT

British Aerospace has teamed up with US defence giant Lockheed Martin to form a $100 billion programme aimed at creating the next generation of light fighter aircraft for the 21st century. BAe had also been in talks with Boeing but chose Lockheed, fuelling speculation that the two companies may merge in the long-term. Lockheed has offered BAe a 12 percent share of the development and production work on the fighter jet programme.
-- INDEPENDENT SUPPLIERS APPLAUD 'REALISTIC' CUT

British independent gas suppliers have applauded the Monopolies and Mergers Commission decision forcing BG Transco to make cuts in the cost for its pipeline transmission. The suppliers believe the cuts will "kick-start" competition in the domestic market of 19 million. Calortex general manager Neil Lambert called the move "good news", noting it was "about time transportation cuts got realistic", while Alan Lias of Beacon Gas echoed the effect the announcement will have on competition, saying the move was "very good news for the customer and us".
-- SMALL FIRMS TO WIN PROTECTION AGAINST FRAUD

British consumer affairs minister Nigel Griffiths said on Wednesday that the government has made plans to bring small businesses under the protection of consumer protection legislation for the first time. The plans permit small businesses to benefit from protections similar to those given to individual customers, including the right to "cooling-off" periods after signing agreements and protection from unfair contracts. Griffiths made the changes in the wake of a series of frauds perpetrated against small businesses.
-- REGULATOR WARNS RAIL OPERATORS TO UPGRADE SYSTEMS

Rail regulator John Swift has begun an attack on UK privatised rail companies over their failure to improve methods of providing customer information and selling tickets, saying that operators could be fined or forced to take immediate remedial action. The regulator is currently conducting a survey of the rail operators involving hundreds of calls to ticket offices and inquiry bureaux, the results of which will be released on Friday. Swift said it was "unacceptable" for rail companies to have not even contributed 'a tenth' of the investment they had promised.
-- 'BBC NEEDS FUNDS' FROM EXTRA DIGITAL TV LICENCE

Leading economists Gavyn Davis of Goldman Sachs and Andrew Graham of Ballihol College, Oxford have argued that the BBC requires a 45-stg per year licence to boost finances and prevent the long-term decline of the corporation. The economists are hoping to be able to pass their findings on to national heritage secretary Chris Smith, saying the supplement should apply to digital satellite, digital cable and digital terrestrial broadcasting and possibly the digital "blackbox" decoders.
-- SIB TEAM ESTABLISHED TO CREATE SINGLE REGULATOR

The Securities and Investments Board has appointed a team to deal with the task of appointing a single regulator for the financial services industry. The team, chaired by SIB's David Pritchard, includes representatives of the Bank of England, the Personal Investment Authority, Securities and Futures Authority, and the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation. The main difficulty faced by the team is the attempt at organising the new SIB in a way that reflects the variety of businesses, products and markets it will regulate, while maintaining input from practitioners and investors.
-- GENCOR SPELLS OUT DETAILS OF LONDON LISTING

South African mining group Gencor has announced it is to list its base metals operations on the London Stock Exchange, a move expected to create a company to be called Billiton worth about 4.2 billion stg. Billiton will also merge with Australian nickel group QNI, a move that creates the world's fourth biggest nickel supplier. Gercor chairman Brian Gilbertson said the stock market listing would free the company from constraints imposed by South African exchange controls.
-- SAINSBURY'S RECRUIT RECEIVED 400,000 STG INCENTIVE

According to Sainsbury's annual report, the supermarket company paid David Bremmer 400,000 stg as incentive to join the company as its chief executive of Homebase and US operations. The payment lifted Bremmer's total pay package to 663,000 stg, the second-largest salary to former managing director David Quarmby, who received 977,000 stg, including 336,000 in compensation for loss of office and 561,000 in pension contributions. Sainsbury defended the incentive as "normal practice...to compensate for loss of benefits from previous employment".
-- INTERNET TECH SPENDS MORE ON INFRASTRUCTURE

Britain's third largest Internet provider, Internet Tech, has reported interim pre-tax losses of 1.17 million stg against one million last time. The results reflect the group's increased spending, necessary to upgrade infrastructure to service its rapid growth. Turnover rose from 360,000 stg to 1.14 million stg, while expenses rose from 884,000 stg to 2.11 million stg. Tech chief executive Laurence Blackall said the results were "in line with expectations".
